transcript.content: Hello, welcome in. I'm Dr. [Name]. To start, can you tell me what brings you in to see me today?

Well, doc, it’s... honestly, it’s because people just keep getting on my case about not listening to them. It’s getting to be a real problem. Like, a major problem. My supervisor down at the plant—I work production, so things move fast, right?—he’ll come up to me, standing right there, looking me dead in the eye, and he'll be talking straight to me about a run or a parts change or something. And I swear I’m looking right back at him, I’m nodding, I'm trying to lock in. But then a minute later, he walks off and I realize I only caught maybe half of what he just said. If that. So then I have to go track him down and ask him to say it all over again, which just pisses him off and makes me look like I don't care about my job. 

And it’s not just work, it’s at home, too. My wife will be sitting across the kitchen table, talking right at me about the bills or the house or whatever, and she gets so mad because she can tell I just missed it. And then it’s this whole big fight, and I have to ask her to repeat herself, and she thinks I’m ignoring her on purpose. But I’m not! I’m sitting right there! It’s just... I don't know, it's like the words just slide right past me, and I'm so sick of everyone being mad at me for it, so my wife finally told me I needed to come see someone.
Has this trouble following what people say been something you've dealt with since you were a kid, or is this a new problem that's really only started recently?

Oh, man, no... definitely not new. Not by a long shot. If you ask my mom, she’ll tell you I’ve been like this pretty much since the day I learned to walk. 

But yeah, especially in school, even way back before I ever hit middle school, I was always the kid getting on everyone's nerves. I mean, I remember my teachers—like Mrs. Gable in third grade, she was this older lady, real strict, you know?—she was constantly having to move my desk. It was like a weekly routine. First I'm in the back row, then I'm up front right next to her desk, then I'm over by the door, then I'm isolated in the corner. She moved me everywhere because I just... I couldn't stay put in my seat to save my life. It was like I had this motor running inside me that just wouldn't shut off. 

And it wasn't just the getting up and wandering around, either. She'd be up there at the chalkboard asking a question to the class, and before she even finished asking it, I’d just blurt out the answer. I wouldn't even think to raise my hand, I just couldn't hold the words in. It drove her absolutely nuts. And the other kids, too—I was always getting into trouble because I’d get bored, and then I’d be leaning over, butting right into whatever the kid next to me was working on. I'd be grabbing their pencils or telling them how to do their math worksheet, just totally invading their space. I just couldn't mind my own business. So yeah, this whole thing of people getting frustrated with me... it's been going on pretty much my whole life, way back to when I was just a little kid.

final_diagnosis.reason: The patient presents with a lifelong pattern (since early childhood, confirmed by both current report and childhood history via teacher/parent observations) of significant inattention (failing to follow conversations/instructions, needing repetition, appearing not to listen despite direct engagement) combined with hyperactive-impulsive symptoms (inability to stay seated, blurting out answers before questions were finished, intrusiveness with peers, excessive motor restlessness described as 'a motor running inside me'). Symptoms are pervasive across multiple settings (work, home, and historically school), causing functional impairment in occupational and marital relationships, with clear childhood onset. This combined presentation of both inattentive and hyperactive-impulsive symptom clusters, persisting into adulthood with cross-situational impairment, supports a diagnosis of Attention-Deficit Hyperactivity Disorder, Combined Type (F90.0), rather than a purely inattentive or hyperactive-impulsive subtype.
